messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Editor
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 56

It began eighteen months ago, on a humid July evening. Arjun walks home from the metro, earphones in, when the intersection ahead erupts. A black SUV mounts the curb. Officers shout through bullhorns. A young man in a grey hoodie stands frozen in the crosswalk, hands raised, then drops to his knees. The air fills with the staccato of commands, then the heavy, wet sounds Arjun will not name out loud. He does not run. He stands paralyzed in a crowd of strangers, watching the red taillights of the SUV swallow the scene. The days that follow blur into a fog of news alerts, neighborly whispers, and a press conference that offers flat condolences. But for Arjun, the world does not return to its previous shape. Sleep becomes a negotiation he consistently loses. His bedroom ceiling transforms into a screen. He lies awake, counting the seconds between car backfires and his own hammering pulse, waiting for the next siren that never comes. Daylight offers little refuge. When the city news broadcasts a routine traffic stop, his stomach tightens until he has to leave the room. He stops watching the evening news altogether. At work, his editors notice the shift. His meticulous eye for narrative detail, once his greatest asset, now works against him. Every mention of a badge, a siren, or a crowded street in the manuscripts he reviews triggers a physical recoil. He begins requesting only literary fiction and historical essays, claiming a creative preference, though he knows it is something closer to preservation. The white spaces on his proofreading sheets multiply. Paragraphs cross themselves out before he even finishes them. Now, at twenty-six, he sits at his desk, the blue light of two monitors washing over his face. His posture carries the weight of someone who has forgotten how to lean back. On the screen, a manuscript for a crime thriller sits open. He reads the same paragraph fourteen times this morning. His eyes trace the lines, but the words dissolve into static. He closes the document, tells himself he will return to it later, and walks to the window. He checks the locks on his apartment door for the third time. Maya leaves a cup of chai on the edge of his desk and touches his shoulder. He flinches, just barely, before forcing his shoulders down. “I’m fine,” he says, and turns back to the screen. Maya tries to bridge the gap. She suggests weekend drives to the lake, knowing he needs space, knowing he also needs her. He goes to the edge of the parking lot and stares at the treeline, his jaw working silently. At family dinners, his mother’s questions about when they will start a household feel impossibly distant. He nods, smiles, and changes the subject to work, though the work has become a maze of crossed-out text. He tells himself he is rebuilding. He buys noise-canceling headphones. He schedules runs along the river at dawn, when the roads are empty and the world is still soft with mist. But the quiet does not last. When the city wakes, so does the watchfulness. He scans the street for unmarked vehicles. He notes the positions of exit signs in every restaurant. He counts the doors in his building. At gatherings, the sounds of children chasing each other in the courtyard send a cold jolt through his ribs. He stands near the doorway, one hand resting on the frame, listening to the room fade into the background. He loves Maya. He loves her deeply. But when she reaches for his hand in a dark theater, his muscles lock, and he has to gently disentangle himself, whispering that his arm is asleep, that it is nothing. He returns to his desk. The cursor blinks. He opens the manuscript again, and begins to read.
